extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of constitutional law and political theory; policymakers and informed public interested in bicameral legislatures
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate the purpose, virtues, and defects of an upper/revising chamber (e.g., the House of Lords) — what structural and behavioural features make a second chamber useful or harmful in a constitution. Emphasises practical examples (Reform Act 1832, Corn Laws, colonial legislatures, federal senates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Available sovereign authority / 'come-at-able' power
rubrics_metrics.description: "There ought to be 'in every Constitution an available authority somewhere. The sovereign power must be come-at-able.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained with the example that the Crown's power to create new peers (threat of swamping) made the Lords yield at Reform 1832; the mere existence of such a power can be as useful as its exercise — a structural safety-valve to prevent permanent obstruction by an upper chamber.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of two co‑equal Houses of distinct natures
rubrics_metrics.description: "The evil of two co-equal Houses of distinct natures is obvious... Each House can stop all legislation, and yet some legislation may be necessary."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning that co‑ordinate authority in two differently constituted chambers invites deadlock (US and Swiss examples). Critiques the federal doctrine that equal veto for unequal states is self-evident — equality of veto can create a dangerous impasse rather than sound government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function as a revising and suspending chamber (hypothetical veto)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Since the Reform Act the House of Lords has become a revising and suspending House. It can alter Bills; it can reject Bills on which the House of Commons is not yet thoroughly in earnest... Their veto is a sort of hypothetical veto."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical role: alter, delay, or reject bills temporarily to test seriousness of Commons/nation. Example language: "We reject your Bill for this once, or these twice... but if you keep on sending it up... we won't reject it." Emphasises measured, non‑permanent obstruction rather than absolute veto.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from social bribe; capacity for disinterested judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: "The House of Lords, as a body, is accessible to no social bribe... They are above corruption because they are the corrupters. They have no constituency to fear or wheedle; they have the best means of forming a disinterested and cool judgment."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independence arises from absence of electoral constituency and press/position pressures. This enables cooler, less populist judgments and reduces susceptibility to the kinds of corruption that affect Commons members and influential journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leisure to revise intellectually
rubrics_metrics.description: "They have, too, leisure to form it... Politics are the only occupation a peer has worth the name. He may pursue them undistractedly."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peers' relative leisure (no distracting occupations) gives them time for careful intellectual revision and judicial consideration of legislation — a key justification for a revising chamber when the lower house lacks time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different composition to check narrow/selfish interests in the Commons
rubrics_metrics.description: "A casual majority of the House of Commons has therefore dominant power... There are said to be two hundred members 'for the railways'... a second chamber of an opposite sort... in which that interest in all likelihood will not rule."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A revising chamber should be composed so that it is unlikely to be captured by the same narrow or selfish coalitions that can dominate the Commons (e.g., sectional economic interests). Its differing composition provides a brake on minor or technical abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visible diligence and active assembly (avoid apathy/'tapestry')
rubrics_metrics.description: "An assembly — a revising assembly especially — which does not assemble, which looks as if it does not care how it revises, is defective... 'the cure for admiring the House of Lords was to go and look at it' — perhaps ten peers in the House, possibly only six; three is the quorum."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attendance, active participation, and visible seriousness are necessary for legitimacy. A revising chamber that is habitually absent or apathetic undermines public confidence and cannot convincingly fulfil revision duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not to be expected to resist popular revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is idle to expect a second chamber — a chamber of notables — ever to resist a popular chamber, a nation's chamber, when that chamber is vehement and the nation vehement too."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies the realistic role: an upper house is not a reliable bulwark against determined popular movements or revolutionary change; its purpose is stability and revision under normal conditions, not suppression of mass will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid depriving the lower house of its best leaders (colonial caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: "In those colonies there were hardly enough good people for one assembly, and not near enough good people for two assemblies... The second assembly was either the nominee of the Crown... or was elected by people with a higher property qualification... The popular assembly was denuded of those guides and leaders who would have led and guided it best."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A second chamber that siphons off the best talent from the popular chamber can weaken representative government — especially in small or developing polities. Design must consider population size and availability of qualified legislators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical possibility and social respectability as prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: "The House of Lords has the greatest merit which such a chamber can have; it is possible... It is incredibly difficult to get a revising assembly, because it is difficult to find a class of respected revisers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A revising chamber must be credible and respected in society to function effectively. Federal senates can succeed by embodying strong local/state feelings; in other contexts it is hard to create an impopular but effective revising body.
